ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, a wooden board with mass $M=1\mathrm{kg}$ is at rest on a rough horizontal ground. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the board and the ground is $\mu_{1}=0.1$. A small iron block with mass $m=1\mathrm{kg}$ and negligible size is placed at the left end of the board. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the iron block and the board is $\mu_{2}=0.4$. Take $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. If a pulling force of magnitude $F=1\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the right end of the iron block, determine the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the iron block.
2. If a pulling force of magnitude $F=5\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the right end of the iron block, determine the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the iron block.
3. If the length of the wooden board is $L=1\mathrm{m}$, and a constant horizontal force $F=8\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the iron block to the right, how long will it take for the iron block to move to the right end of the board?

The magnitude of friction that can be provided between the wooden plank and the ground is calculated as mu1(M+m)g=0.1*2*10=2 N; the maximum friction between the iron block and the wooden plank is calculated as mu2*m*g=0.4*1*10=4 N. 1) When F=1 N, the external force is less than the 2 N that the ground friction can balance, so the system can remain at rest; therefore the magnitude of the friction force exerted on the iron block by the wooden plank is equal to the pulling force, which is 1 N. 2) When F=5 N, if the iron block and the wooden plank do not slide relative to each other, regard the two as a whole, then the acceleration a=(5-2)/(1+1)=1.5 m/s^2. Write the equation for the iron block: 5-f=1*1.5, so f=3.5 N. Because 3.5 N<4 N, the no-sliding assumption holds, so the magnitude of the friction force on the iron block is 3.5 N. 3) When F=8 N, if there is no sliding, the overall acceleration is (8-2)/2=3 m/s^2, and the friction required by the iron block is f=8-1*3=5 N, which is greater than 4 N, so the iron block slides relative to the wooden plank. At this time, the magnitude of the kinetic friction force exerted on the iron block by the wooden plank is 4 N, directed leftward; the wooden plank is subjected to a friction force of 4 N from the iron block rightward, and at the same time is subjected to ground friction of 2 N leftward. The acceleration of the iron block a_block=(8-4)/1=4 m/s^2, the acceleration of the wooden plank a_board=(4-2)/1=2 m/s^2, and the relative acceleration is 2 m/s^2. From the left end to the right end requires a relative displacement L=1 m, and the initial relative velocity is 0, so 1=(1/2)*2*t^2, giving t=1 s.

raw_record.question_text:
As shown in the figure, a wooden board with mass $M=1\mathrm{kg}$ is at rest on a rough horizontal ground. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the board and the ground is $\mu_{1}=0.1$. A small iron block with mass $m=1\mathrm{kg}$ and negligible size is placed at the left end of the board. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the iron block and the board is $\mu_{2}=0.4$. Take $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. If a pulling force of magnitude $F=1\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the right end of the iron block, determine the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the iron block.
2. If a pulling force of magnitude $F=5\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the right end of the iron block, determine the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the iron block.
3. If the length of the wooden board is $L=1\mathrm{m}$, and a constant horizontal force $F=8\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the iron block to the right, how long will it take for the iron block to move to the right end of the board?

method.method_draft: First describe the figure: a small block labeled m sits at the left end of a long wooden board labeled M, and the board rests on a rough horizontal floor; the board length L is marked from the left end to the right end. Take rightward as positive. From the text read M=m=1 kg, μ1=0.1 for board-ground, μ2=0.4 for block-board, g=10 m/s², and the three applied forces. Compute limiting frictions: ground contact can supply/use 0.1(M+m)g=2 N when the board is loaded by both masses, and block-board limiting friction is 0.4mg=4 N. For F=1 N, compare with the 2 N ground threshold: the whole system can remain at rest, so the friction on the block simply balances the pull, giving 1 N. For F=5 N, assume no slip between block and board and treat the two bodies as one system moving against 2 N ground friction: a=(5-2)/(1+1)=1.5 m/s². Then apply Newton’s second law to the block: 5-f=1·1.5, so f=3.5 N; check 3.5<4, so no slip is consistent. For F=8 N, the no-slip required friction would be f=8-[(8-2)/2]=5 N, exceeding 4 N, so the block slips. Use kinetic friction f=4 N on the block leftward and on the board rightward; board-ground friction is 2 N leftward. Thus a_block=(8-4)/1=4 m/s² and a_board=(4-2)/1=2 m/s², so relative acceleration is 2 m/s². Starting from the left end, the block must gain relative displacement L=1 m: 1=(1/2)(2)t², so t=1 s.

method.method_draft: First read the diagram as a contact stack: block m on top of board M, board on floor, with the block starting at the left end and needing to reach the right end over distance L. Build a piecewise force-response model as a function of applied pull F. The ground support carries both weights, so the board-ground friction scale is μ1(M+m)g=2 N; the maximum block-board friction scale is μ2mg=4 N. Region I: if F≤2 N, the ground can hold the board/system at rest, so the block friction equals F. Therefore for F=1 N, the friction on the block is 1 N. Region II: if the board moves but the block does not slip on it, the two masses have common acceleration a=(F-2)/(M+m). The friction required on the block is f=F-ma. With M=m=1, this gives f=F-(F-2)/2=(F+2)/2. The no-slip condition f≤4 gives F≤6 N. Since F=5 N is in this region, f=(5+2)/2=3.5 N. Region III: if F>6 N, the block slips, so the block-board friction is fixed at 4 N. For F=8 N, compute a_block=8-4=4 m/s² and a_board=4-2=2 m/s², hence a_rel=2 m/s². Use the visual starting condition at the left end and the marked distance L=1 m: L=(1/2)a_rel t², giving t=1 s.

method.method_draft: First describe the figure: the small mass m is at the board’s left edge, the board M rests on the rough horizontal surface, and the length L marked along the board is the relative travel needed to reach the right edge. Use a free-body-equation method with unknown interface friction f and solve by consistency. For F=1 N, write static equilibrium: the pull on the block must be opposed by friction from the board; because 1 N is below the available block-board limit 4 N and the ground can oppose the transmitted force up to 2 N, the block friction magnitude is 1 N. For F=5 N, impose the no-relative-motion constraint suggested by checking whether the block can stick to the board: both bodies have acceleration a. The block equation is F-f=ma, and the board equation is f-2=Ma, where 2 N is the floor friction. With M=m=1 and F=5, solve the two equations simultaneously: 5-f=a and f-2=a, giving f=3.5 N and a=1.5 m/s²; since f<4 N, the sticking assumption is valid. For F=8 N, the same simultaneous sticking equations would give f=5 N, which violates the 4 N contact limit; therefore set f=4 N. Then write separate equations: block, 8-4=a_m; board, 4-2=a_M. This yields a_m=4 m/s² and a_M=2 m/s². The relative acceleration is a_m-a_M=2 m/s², so the time to cover the visually indicated length L=1 m is found from 1=(1/2)(2)t², giving t=1 s.

raw_record.original_question:
As shown in the figure, a wooden board with mass $M=1\mathrm{kg}$ is at rest on a rough horizontal ground. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the board and the ground is $\mu_{1}=0.1$. A small iron block with mass $m=1\mathrm{kg}$ and negligible size is placed at the left end of the board. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the iron block and the board is $\mu_{2}=0.4$. Take $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. If a pulling force of magnitude $F=1\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the right end of the iron block, determine the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the iron block.
2. If a pulling force of magnitude $F=5\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the right end of the iron block, determine the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the iron block.
3. If the length of the wooden board is $L=1\mathrm{m}$, and a constant horizontal force $F=8\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the iron block to the right, how long will it take for the iron block to move to the right end of the board?
raw_record.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, a small iron block is labeled m and is placed at the far left end of a long wooden plank; the long wooden plank is labeled M and is placed horizontally on rough ground; the length of the wooden plank from the left end to the right end is labeled L. Reasoning: Take rightward as positive. It is known that M=1 kg, m=1 kg, mu1=0.1, mu2=0.4, g=10 m/s^2. The magnitude of friction that can be provided between the wooden plank and the ground is calculated as mu1(M+m)g=0.1*2*10=2 N; the maximum friction between the iron block and the wooden plank is calculated as mu2*m*g=0.4*1*10=4 N. 1) When F=1 N, the external force is less than the 2 N that the ground friction can balance, so the system can remain at rest; therefore the magnitude of the friction force exerted on the iron block by the wooden plank is equal to the pulling force, which is 1 N. 2) When F=5 N, if the iron block and the wooden plank do not slide relative to each other, regard the two as a whole, then the acceleration a=(5-2)/(1+1)=1.5 m/s^2. Write the equation for the iron block: 5-f=1*1.5, so f=3.5 N. Because 3.5 N<4 N, the no-sliding assumption holds, so the magnitude of the friction force on the iron block is 3.5 N. 3) When F=8 N, if there is no sliding, the overall acceleration is (8-2)/2=3 m/s^2, and the friction required by the iron block is f=8-1*3=5 N, which is greater than 4 N, so the iron block slides relative to the wooden plank. At this time, the magnitude of the kinetic friction force exerted on the iron block by the wooden plank is 4 N, directed leftward; the wooden plank is subjected to a friction force of 4 N from the iron block rightward, and at the same time is subjected to ground friction of 2 N leftward. The acceleration of the iron block a_block=(8-4)/1=4 m/s^2, the acceleration of the wooden plank a_board=(4-2)/1=2 m/s^2, and the relative acceleration is 2 m/s^2. From the left end to the right end requires a relative displacement L=1 m, and the initial relative velocity is 0, so 1=(1/2)*2*t^2, giving t=1 s.

The magnitude of friction that can be provided between the wooden plank and the ground is calculated as mu1(M+m)g=0.1*2*10=2 N; the maximum friction between the iron block and the wooden plank is calculated as mu2*m*g=0.4*1*10=4 N. 1) When F=1 N, the external force is less than the 2 N that the ground friction can balance, so the system can remain at rest; therefore the magnitude of the friction force exerted on the iron block by the wooden plank is equal to the pulling force, which is 1 N. 2) When F=5 N, if the iron block and the wooden plank do not slide relative to each other, regard the two as a whole, then the acceleration a=(5-2)/(1+1)=1.5 m/s^2. Write the equation for the iron block: 5-f=1*1.5, so f=3.5 N. Because 3.5 N<4 N, the no-sliding assumption holds, so the magnitude of the friction force on the iron block is 3.5 N. 3) When F=8 N, if there is no sliding, the overall acceleration is (8-2)/2=3 m/s^2, and the friction required by the iron block is f=8-1*3=5 N, which is greater than 4 N, so the iron block slides relative to the wooden plank. At this time, the magnitude of the kinetic friction force exerted on the iron block by the wooden plank is 4 N, directed leftward; the wooden plank is subjected to a friction force of 4 N from the iron block rightward, and at the same time is subjected to ground friction of 2 N leftward. The acceleration of the iron block a_block=(8-4)/1=4 m/s^2, the acceleration of the wooden plank a_board=(4-2)/1=2 m/s^2, and the relative acceleration is 2 m/s^2. From the left end to the right end requires a relative displacement L=1 m, and the initial relative velocity is 0, so 1=(1/2)*2*t^2, giving t=1 s.
